title: the gods who borrowed their glory
word: the Gayatri and the peace chants
hookLine: a friend's good news, and the Kena's gods who couldn't burn a straw
carry: all shining is brahman's light, borrowed
tomorrow: one person, alone at a window. so why does the verse say we?

cards: Somebody's good news lands in the group chat: early acceptance, dream school, a row of exclamation points. It's possible to be truly glad for a friend and still, for one second, feel a little dimmer.
Priya had that second this week. It's a good second to meet the Gayatri's next words: bhargo devasya. The radiance of the god.

teach.b: Its full form is bhargas, and before the d of devasya it turns to o. Devasya: of the god. So, the radiance of the god, and the first line's that finally lands.
Now a story about whose shining it is. In the Kena Upanishad, the gods win a great victory, and they start to boast: this victory is ours, this glory is ours.
Then a strange spirit appears in front of them, and they can't tell what it is.
Agni, the fire, walks up: I can burn anything on earth. The spirit sets down one blade of straw. Burn this.
Agni can't. Vayu, the wind: I can carry off anything. He can't move the straw.
Then Indra goes, and the spirit vanishes, and in its place stands a radiant woman, Uma, daughter of the Himalaya. She tells him: that was Brahman.
The victory you were proud of was Brahman's. That's the teaching: no one's shine is their own.

teach.h: BY ITS LIGHT ALL THIS SHINES.
teach.b: The Katha Upanishad puts it in one line: everything shines after that one shining; by its light all this shines. Many teachers read the Gayatri's bhargo devasya that way: not my radiance, not yours, the god's.
Which changes Priya's dim second. Anika's news isn't light taken from her. It's the same light, shining through someone else today.

how: Teachers who explain the Gayatri often pause on bhargo devasya, the radiance of the god; some read it alongside the Kena Upanishad's story and the Katha's line that all things shine by one light. At arati, families wave a lamp before the deity, offering light back.

games.q: what does “the gayatri and the peace chants” mean?
o: a contest where Agni burns down a forest
a goddess who steals the sun's light
boasting gods, one blade of straw, and whose light it really is

p: fire, who couldn't burn one straw
who told Indra the victory was Brahman's
by its light all this shines

s: in the Kena, Agni burns the straw to prove his power
he couldn't. the power was never his; it was Brahman's.
bhargo and bhargas are the same word
bhargas turns to bhargo before the d of devasya.
devasya means of the gods, plural
it's singular: of the god, a title for Savitr.

games.q: your little brother asks why the fire god couldn't burn one piece of straw. which answer is the Kena's teaching?
o: the fire's power was never its own; it was Brahman's.
the straw was wet from the battle.
Agni was tired and needed a rest.
games.why: Uma told Indra the gods' victory was Brahman's. many teachers read the Gayatri's radiance of the god the same way: a light nobody owns.

practice: If there's a lamp or a diya at home, light it and move it gently in a small circle, the way families do at arati, giving the light back to the one it came from.
If not, count on your fingers people whose light you've seen by lately, and give each one a breath. Stop at five, or wherever the time runs out.

wordCard.voice: The Gayatri and the peace chants. Today's piece: bhargo devasya, the radiance of the god, a light nobody owns.

orig.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: bhargo devasya, the radiance of the god.

carryVoice: Your line: all shining is Brahman's light, borrowed, Anika's and yours alike. That's today.
